contactZones.name: The Silk Roads
contactZones.flows: Silk, paper, horses, Buddhism, Islam, Manichaeism, Nestorian Christianity, music and plague
contactZones.hook: A caravanserai where five faiths share one well; a scribe who carries a forbidden sutra west.

contactZones.name: Indian Ocean monsoon world
contactZones.flows: Dhows riding the monsoon; Swahili coast trade; Islam, Hinduism and Buddhism; spices, cloth, porcelain, enslaved people
contactZones.hook: A Swahili navigator, a Gujarati merchant and a Chinese admiral (Zheng He's fleets) in one harbour.

contactZones.name: Trans-Saharan routes
contactZones.flows: Gold, salt, books, Islam and scholarship (Timbuktu); camel caravans
contactZones.hook: A Timbuktu manuscript-keeper smuggling a library across the dunes.

contactZones.name: The Atlantic world & African diaspora
contactZones.flows: The trade in enslaved Africans; resistance and maroon nations; Orisha, Vodun and Kongo faiths reborn; creole languages
contactZones.hook: A Kongo nkisi tradition remade as Palo in Cuba; Yoruba Ifá reaching Bahia and Havana.

contactZones.name: Austronesian voyaging
contactZones.flows: Outrigger and double-hulled canoes from Taiwan to Madagascar to Rapa Nui; wayfinding; shared words across half the planet
contactZones.hook: A Malagasy and a Hawaiian discovering they share the word for ‘eye’ (maso / maka).

contactZones.name: The Manila galleons
contactZones.flows: Silver from Mexico, silk and porcelain from China via Manila; Filipino settlers in Mexico; Chavacano
contactZones.hook: A Filipino sailor who jumps ship in Acapulco and starts a new lineage.

contactZones.name: The Nile corridor
contactZones.flows: Egypt, Kush/Nubia and Ethiopia: pharaohs, Kandakes, Christian Nubian kingdoms, Ge'ez learning
contactZones.hook: A Kushite queen negotiating with Rome; a Nubian church painter in medieval Faras.

contactZones.name: The Eurasian steppe
contactZones.flows: Horse cultures, Scythians, Huns, Turks, Mongols; epic singers; Tengri
contactZones.hook: A Mongol messenger carrying a paiza tablet from Karakorum to the Danube.

contactZones.name: Buddhist transmission
contactZones.flows: Monks, pilgrims (Xuanzang), translated sutras, temple art
contactZones.hook: A pilgrim monk who returns with texts no one can yet read.

contactZones.name: The Persianate world
contactZones.flows: Persian as court language from Istanbul to Bengal; miniature painting; Sufi poetry
contactZones.hook: A Mughal court poet writing in Persian about a Rajput princess.

contactZones.name: Qhapaq Ñan (Inca road system)
contactZones.flows: Roads, relay runners (chaskis), khipu messages across the Andes
contactZones.hook: A chaski runner who memorised a khipu meant for a dead emperor.

contactZones.name: Mississippian & Hopewell exchange
contactZones.flows: Copper, shells and obsidian traded across North America; Cahokia mound city
contactZones.hook: A trader from the Gulf coast arriving at Cahokia's great plaza.

contactZones.name: Circumpolar & Bering world
contactZones.flows: Reindeer herding, shared shamanic traditions, trade across the Bering Strait
contactZones.hook: Yupik families with kin on both sides of the Bering Strait.

contactZones.name: Tea-Horse & Himalayan salt roads
contactZones.flows: Tea for horses, salt for grain; caravans over high passes
contactZones.hook: A Naxi caravan leader caught in a winter pass with a monk and a smuggler.

contactZones.name: Hajj & pilgrimage routes
contactZones.flows: Pilgrims, scholars and merchants; Mansa Musa's 1324 hajj
contactZones.hook: A Hausa scholar who walks to Mecca and returns years later, transformed.

contactZones.name: Indian indenture
contactZones.flows: Girmitiya labourers to Trinidad, Guyana, Fiji, Mauritius and Natal; chutney music, Bhojpuri, Hindu and Muslim festivals abroad
contactZones.hook: A girmitiya woman who keeps her village songs alive in Fiji.

contactZones.name: Chinese Nanyang & Pacific diasporas
contactZones.flows: Peranakan cultures, Chinatowns, Tusán Peru, Chinese Cuba
contactZones.hook: A Peranakan matriarch in Penang running a spice empire.

contactZones.name: Levantine & Lebanese diasporas
contactZones.flows: Merchants in Senegal, Brazil, Mexico; Maronite, Orthodox and Druze communities abroad
contactZones.hook: A Lebanese-Senegalese family navigating independence.

contactZones.name: Romani migration
contactZones.flows: A people originating in north India, travelling through Persia and the Byzantine world into Europe; Romani language keeps Indic roots
contactZones.hook: A Romani family whose words still echo Sanskrit.

contactZones.name: Sephardic & Jewish diasporas
contactZones.flows: Expulsion from Iberia (1492); Ladino; Jewish communities from Kaifeng to Cochin to Ethiopia
contactZones.hook: A Ladino-speaking printer in Ottoman Salonica.

contactZones.name: Caribbean exile & Garifuna
contactZones.flows: Afro-Indigenous Garifuna exiled from St Vincent to Central America
contactZones.hook: A Garifuna drummer keeping Kalinago words alive in Honduras.

contactZones.name: Oman–Zanzibar & Swahili coast
contactZones.flows: Omani sultanate in Zanzibar; Ibadi Islam; clove plantations; Swahili poetry
contactZones.hook: A Swahili poet writing in Arabic script for an Omani court.

contactZones.name: Pacific blackbirding & colonial routes
contactZones.flows: Coerced labour of Pacific Islanders in Queensland, Peru and Fiji; Tok Pisin and Bislama born from plantation life
contactZones.hook: Ni-Vanuatu sailors who bring back a new language.

contactZones.name: The Mediterranean
contactZones.flows: Phoenicians, Carthage, Rome, al-Andalus, Ottoman fleets; Sabir lingua franca
contactZones.hook: A Moorish astronomer and a Jewish translator in Toledo.

contactZones.name: The Great Migration
contactZones.flows: Six million Black Southerners moved north and west; the Harlem Renaissance, Chicago blues, new churches and newspapers
contactZones.hook: A blues singer who carries her grandmother's root bag from Mississippi to the South Side.

contactZones.name: The Underground Railroad
contactZones.flows: Freedom seekers to the North, Canada, Mexico and maroon communities in swamps and Seminole lands
contactZones.hook: A conductor who reads the stars and the songs at once.

contactZones.name: Return to Africa
contactZones.flows: Black Loyalists to Sierra Leone, African Americans to Liberia, Afro-Brazilian Agudá and Tabom to the Bight of Benin
contactZones.hook: A Krio family that remembers both Nova Scotia snow and Freetown rain.

contactZones.name: Windrush & the Caribbean in Britain
contactZones.flows: Caribbean migrants rebuilding post-war Britain; sound systems, carnival, the 2018 Windrush scandal
contactZones.hook: A Notting Hill carnival band leader keeping her island's mas alive.

contactZones.name: The Haitian Revolution's ripples
contactZones.flows: The first free Black republic; refugees to Louisiana and Cuba; hope and fear across the Atlantic world
contactZones.hook: A New Orleans healer who fled Saint-Domingue with a secret.

powerArchetypes.name: Cultivation ladder
powerArchetypes.roots: Daoist inner alchemy (neidan) and its modern xianxia descendants
powerArchetypes.summary: Power refined through breath, discipline and stages of realisation.
powerArchetypes.structure: Stages or realms; bottlenecks; sects; elixirs; heavenly tribulations
powerArchetypes.prompts: Name each stage; what blocks advancement; what a failed breakthrough costs.
powerArchetypes.care: Draw on real Daoist ideas respectfully; xianxia is a genre, Daoism a living faith.

powerArchetypes.name: Àṣẹ — power to make it so
powerArchetypes.roots: Yoruba thought
powerArchetypes.summary: The authority and force that makes things happen, held by gods, words and people.
powerArchetypes.prompts: Who holds àṣẹ? How is it spent or grown?
powerArchetypes.care: Living religious concept; consult Yoruba sources.

powerArchetypes.name: Nyama — energy released by action
powerArchetypes.roots: Mande (Mali) thought
powerArchetypes.summary: Every deed releases a force that must be handled; smiths and griots are its specialists.
powerArchetypes.structure: Consequences that pile up; specialists who manage them
powerArchetypes.prompts: What does each act release? Who is trained to channel it?

powerArchetypes.name: Mana — prestige-power
powerArchetypes.roots: Polynesian and Melanesian cultures
powerArchetypes.summary: Power and prestige that can be gained, lost or transferred through deeds and lineage.
powerArchetypes.prompts: How is mana lost? What tapu protects it?
powerArchetypes.care: Concept varies by culture; avoid flattening into ‘magic points’.

powerArchetypes.name: Tapas — ascetic heat
powerArchetypes.roots: Vedic and Hindu tradition
powerArchetypes.summary: Austerity generates heat-power strong enough to shake the gods; boons follow.
powerArchetypes.prompts: What austerity, for how long? What loophole hides in the boon?

powerArchetypes.name: Siddhis — perfections
powerArchetypes.roots: Yoga, Tantra and Buddhist traditions
powerArchetypes.summary: Extraordinary powers (becoming tiny, weightless, knowing others' minds) as side-effects of practice — often warned against.
powerArchetypes.structure: Mastery as a by-product, not the goal
powerArchetypes.prompts: Why might a master refuse to use their powers?

powerArchetypes.name: Baraka — transferable blessing
powerArchetypes.roots: Islamic and Maghrebi / Sufi traditions
powerArchetypes.summary: Blessing-power flowing from God through saints, places and objects; it can be passed on.
powerArchetypes.structure: Saints' tombs; lineages of sheikhs; touched objects
powerArchetypes.prompts: How does baraka pass? Can it be misused?
powerArchetypes.care: Treat Islamic concepts with respect; avoid ‘evil marabout’ tropes.

powerArchetypes.name: Hamingja — family luck-spirit
powerArchetypes.roots: Norse belief
powerArchetypes.summary: Luck as a guardian spirit that follows a family and can be lent or inherited.
powerArchetypes.prompts: Who inherits the luck? What happens when it is lent?
powerArchetypes.care: Reject white-supremacist misuse of Norse imagery.

powerArchetypes.name: Kotodama — spirit of words
powerArchetypes.roots: Japanese belief
powerArchetypes.summary: Words carry spirit; speaking shapes reality, so some words are avoided.
powerArchetypes.prompts: Which words are dangerous? Who may speak names?

powerArchetypes.name: Sacred sound & praise poetry
powerArchetypes.roots: Mantra (South Asia), izibongo (Zulu), oríkì (Yoruba)
powerArchetypes.summary: Correctly spoken sound or praise empowers people, gods and places.
powerArchetypes.prompts: What happens if the sound is wrong?

powerArchetypes.name: Spirit relationships & possession
powerArchetypes.roots: Orisha, lwa, tromba, mudang, hầu đồng traditions
powerArchetypes.summary: Practitioners host or partner with spirits who act through them.
powerArchetypes.prompts: What does each spirit want? What does the host give up?
powerArchetypes.care: These are living religions: never reduce them to horror tropes.

powerArchetypes.name: Ancestral intercession
powerArchetypes.roots: Widespread across Africa, Asia and the Americas
powerArchetypes.summary: Ancestors act for the living when honoured.
powerArchetypes.prompts: Which ancestor answers? What do they demand?

powerArchetypes.name: Craft as power
powerArchetypes.roots: Smiths (Mande, Ogun, Ilmarinen, Hephaestus), weavers, potters
powerArchetypes.summary: Making things is sacred and dangerous; makers form guarded lineages.
powerArchetypes.prompts: What is the secret of the craft? Why is it feared?
powerArchetypes.care: Craft lineages can overlap with caste; handle with care.

powerArchetypes.name: Name power
powerArchetypes.roots: Ancient Egyptian ren, folk traditions worldwide
powerArchetypes.summary: Knowing a true name gives power over its bearer.
powerArchetypes.prompts: Who knows your true name?

powerArchetypes.name: Divination systems
powerArchetypes.roots: Ifá, I Ching, sikidy, geomancy (ʿilm al-raml), astrology, tarot
powerArchetypes.summary: Structured systems for reading fate; the reading carries obligations.
powerArchetypes.structure: Corpus of meanings; specialists; prescribed actions
powerArchetypes.prompts: What must you do after a reading?

powerArchetypes.name: Landscape power
powerArchetypes.roots: Feng shui, songlines, sacred geography
powerArchetypes.summary: Power flows through land; placement and movement matter.
powerArchetypes.prompts: Where does the power pool? Who owns the land?
powerArchetypes.care: Songlines belong to Aboriginal nations; invent your own geography.

powerArchetypes.name: Calendar & star power
powerArchetypes.roots: Maya tzolk'in day-signs, Hindu nakshatras, Chinese zodiac
powerArchetypes.summary: Your day or star of birth shapes your gifts.
powerArchetypes.prompts: What can only be done on certain days?

powerArchetypes.name: Animal counterpart
powerArchetypes.roots: Mesoamerican nahualli, totemic ideas worldwide
powerArchetypes.summary: A person shares a soul or fate with an animal.
powerArchetypes.prompts: What happens to you when your counterpart is hurt?
powerArchetypes.care: Totemic systems are culture-specific; avoid generic ‘spirit animals’.

powerArchetypes.name: Alchemy & transmutation
powerArchetypes.roots: Jabir ibn Hayyan, Chinese waidan, Indian rasayana
powerArchetypes.summary: Transforming matter (and the self) through processes.
powerArchetypes.prompts: What does each transmutation cost?

powerArchetypes.name: Martial internal energy
powerArchetypes.roots: Qi / ki / prana in martial arts (taijiquan, kalaripayattu, silat)
powerArchetypes.summary: Trained energy for strength, healing and striking vital points.
powerArchetypes.prompts: What does a master never teach?

powerArchetypes.name: Conjure & rootwork
powerArchetypes.roots: Hoodoo, Obeah and related African diaspora practices
powerArchetypes.summary: Roots, signs, spoken psalms and crafted charms that protect, heal and turn harm back.
powerArchetypes.structure: Practitioner lineages; ingredients; spoken work; reciprocity
powerArchetypes.prompts: What does the rootworker ask in return? What happens if work is crossed?
powerArchetypes.care: Living practices born of survival — don't villainise them.

powerArchetypes.name: Flight home
powerArchetypes.roots: The Flying Africans legend (Igbo Landing, Gullah, Caribbean tellings); Toni Morrison, Virginia Hamilton
powerArchetypes.summary: Power to rise and return to the ancestral home, born from refusal of bondage.
powerArchetypes.structure: Words that must be remembered; a cost of leaving others behind
powerArchetypes.prompts: Who remembers the words? Who can't fly, and why?
powerArchetypes.care: Rooted in grief and resistance — handle with depth.

powerArchetypes.name: Coded song
powerArchetypes.roots: Spirituals, ring shouts, drum languages, carnival satire
powerArchetypes.summary: Songs that carry hidden instructions, maps and messages past those in power.
powerArchetypes.structure: Double meanings; communities that know the code
powerArchetypes.prompts: What is hidden in the chorus, and who must never understand it?

kinshipTraditions.name: Hānai
kinshipTraditions.description: A child raised by relatives or friends, often grandparents, with open ties to birth parents — an honour, not a rupture.

kinshipTraditions.name: Whāngai
kinshipTraditions.description: Raising a child within the wider whānau to keep knowledge and whakapapa strong.

kinshipTraditions.name: Compadrazgo / kumpare
kinshipTraditions.description: Godparenthood that binds the adults as co-parents with lifelong duties of help and respect.

kinshipTraditions.name: Gaelic fosterage
kinshipTraditions.description: Children of chiefly families raised in other households; foster-siblings were often closer than blood kin.

kinshipTraditions.name: Milk kinship (raḍāʿa)
kinshipTraditions.roots: Islamic law and Arab, Persian, Turkish, Balkan and Caucasian custom
kinshipTraditions.description: Being nursed by the same woman creates kinship, including marriage restrictions.

kinshipTraditions.name: Sworn brotherhood (jiébài)
kinshipTraditions.roots: China — e.g. the Peach Garden Oath in Romance of the Three Kingdoms
kinshipTraditions.description: Unrelated people swear to be siblings, sharing fortune and fate.

kinshipTraditions.name: Pobratimstvo / posestrimstvo
kinshipTraditions.roots: South Slavic sworn brother- and sisterhood
kinshipTraditions.description: A ritual bond, sometimes blessed in church, as strong as blood.

kinshipTraditions.name: Anda
kinshipTraditions.roots: Mongol sworn brotherhood (e.g. Temüjin and Jamukha)
kinshipTraditions.description: Sealed with exchanged gifts and shared blood; betraying an anda is a grave wrong.

kinshipTraditions.name: Age-sets
kinshipTraditions.roots: Maasai, Kikuyu, Oromo (gadaa) and other East African societies
kinshipTraditions.description: People initiated together form a lifelong cohort with shared duties and authority.

kinshipTraditions.name: Guru–shishya paramparā
kinshipTraditions.description: Knowledge passed from teacher to disciple in an unbroken chain, often living together.

kinshipTraditions.name: Sensei–deshi & the iemoto system
kinshipTraditions.description: Arts schools headed by a master household; students can receive names and licences.

kinshipTraditions.name: Senpai–kōhai
kinshipTraditions.description: Senior–junior bonds of guidance and loyalty in schools, clubs and workplaces.

kinshipTraditions.name: Mande artisan apprenticeships
kinshipTraditions.roots: Mande smiths, griots and leatherworkers (West Africa)
kinshipTraditions.description: Secret knowledge passed within specialised families and to chosen apprentices.

kinshipTraditions.name: Padrino / madrina & ojubona
kinshipTraditions.description: Initiators and their assistants become spiritual parents in a religious house.

kinshipTraditions.name: Murshid–murīd & the silsila
kinshipTraditions.description: A spiritual guide leads a disciple along a chain of transmission back to the Prophet.

kinshipTraditions.name: Dharma transmission
kinshipTraditions.roots: Chan, Zen and other Buddhist lineages
kinshipTraditions.description: A master recognises a student as heir, extending a lineage chart.

kinshipTraditions.name: Rav–talmid & chavruta
kinshipTraditions.description: Teacher–student bonds, and study partners who argue texts together for years.

kinshipTraditions.name: Kafala
kinshipTraditions.description: Care and responsibility for a child without changing their lineage or name.

kinshipTraditions.name: Adoption into a nation or clan
kinshipTraditions.roots: Haudenosaunee and many other Native nations
kinshipTraditions.description: Adoption can make someone a full member of a clan and nation. Customs belong to each nation — consult and credit.

kinshipTraditions.name: Classificatory kinship & skin names
kinshipTraditions.description: Everyone is placed in kin relations (e.g. via skin names), shaping who you call mother, brother or avoid. Specifics belong to each nation; do not invent sacred details.

kinshipTraditions.name: Village kin & respect titles
kinshipTraditions.roots: Many African communities (Igbo, Yoruba, Zulu and more)
kinshipTraditions.description: Elders and peers become aunties, uncles and parents by respect and shared responsibility.

kinshipTraditions.name: Fictive kin & church family
kinshipTraditions.description: Play cousins, church mothers and neighbours who are family in every way but blood.

kinshipTraditions.name: Ballroom houses
kinshipTraditions.roots: Black and Latinx LGBTQ+ ballroom culture (New York and beyond)
kinshipTraditions.description: Houses led by house mothers and fathers give chosen families to queer youth.

kinshipTraditions.name: Chosen family
kinshipTraditions.description: Family built by choice and care, especially when birth families reject.

kinshipTraditions.name: Godparents
kinshipTraditions.description: Sponsors who promise spiritual guidance for life.

kinshipTraditions.name: Shipmates (malungo, sippi, mati)
kinshipTraditions.roots: Survivors of the Middle Passage across the Americas
kinshipTraditions.description: People who survived the same slave ship treated one another as kin for life — malungo in Brazil, sippi or mati in Suriname, shipmate in Jamaica and North America.
